doc.title: Bernard Purdie interviewed by Monk Rowe, West Orange, New Jersey, July 30, 2003

chapter: Money and sessions in the sixties
title: Ernie Royal and consequences of his hollering
summary: He used to holler at trumpeter Ernie Royal about wrong notes; some arrangers resented it but kept calling him as he was often contractor.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players

blocks.x: everybody — by this time I mean I’m hot stuff now man. Oh this Bernard Purdie man. I got all this stuff now. I mean I’m good at what I do, people know I’m good at what I do, so I’m going to get the respect of what I say they’re going to try and don’t let me have no frown or something on my face. “Oh my God Purdie don’t like it. He’s the hit maker. If he don’t like it, it ain’t right.” I mean I had that kind of reputation. So I had to keep my reputation going. And as they say the rest becomes history. Because this is what happened. But during those times is when I really started to learn — not to holler across the room at the trumpet player, “You made a mistake at bar four” such and such. Oh my God. Ernie Royal used to want to kill me. I’m serious. Ernie Royal wanted to kill me. Because he was always on the date because I made sure that he was. I mean I was a contractor so I knew who was going to be coming in and such and such. And I used to holler over at him, “Ernie, you know you’re playing the wrong note, why don’t you play the right note at bar” so and so and so and so. And just like that. It was really that simple. That’s what I used to do. And they looked at me and said pay him no mind. He just can’t help himself. He just can’t help himself. And they did. And when the date was over we were all out eating together. We all are doing things together, and such and such and such, and it was over, it was all over, it wasn’t nothing, nothing was held on after the date was over. Ernie might walk up and hit me upside the head, “Purdie leave me alone.” I said, “All right, Ernie, you know I love you, you know I love you.” And never thought anything of it, you know, really. It was over. It was said and done, it was over. I didn’t know that certain arrangers and certain producers really resented that.
And did they start not calling you?

They didn’t stop calling me, not right away. Not until they found somebody else that could do what I was doing. And that took years. By then I had a reputation and somebody else would call me. So I didn’t know that I was losing out on anything, and I didn’t know that I was creating a problem with some of my clients. I just didn’t. But see that was also part of my naiveness. I didn’t mean any harm at what I was doing because I wanted it right. And I felt responsible. Because fifty to sixty percent of those sessions I was the contractor or I was made the leader. So I just wanted it to be right. Always wanted it to be right. So I didn’t think in terms of something being wrong or that I had done something wrong.
Uh huh. You’re just doing your job.
Yeah. And it was a job.
